drapeaux.note: Section VI read on legislation.gov.uk (data.xml of the section): '...for the tearme of fowerteene yeares or under, hereafter to be made of the sole working or makinge of any manner of new Manufactures within this Realme, to the true and first Inventor and Inventors of such Manufactures, which others at the tyme of makinge such tres Patents and Graunts shall not use, soe as alsoe they be not contrary to the Lawe nor mischievous to the State, by raisinge prices of Commodities at home, or hurt of Trade, or generallie inconvenient...'. The quoted phrases 'true and first Inventor' and 'new Manufacture' are fragments of this text; the entry's paraphrase is faithful. Phrases whose source was not reopened (section I wording, Australian Patents Act) were unquoted.

titre: A law against monopolies, and the exception made for the inventor
accroche: In 1624, the English Parliament voids royal monopolies but leaves a door open for the inventor: fourteen years, if he is the first.
contenu_vulgarise:
Under Elizabeth I, the Crown grants by letters patent to a single beneficiary the exclusive right to sell everyday goods, such as starch or salt. The sovereign prizes these privileges because they pay: the beneficiary has to pay dearly for his patent. In 1601, a showdown between the Crown and Parliament puts the examination of these privileges in the hands of the common law courts, but James I keeps granting them. A Parliamentary committee on grievances, chaired by Edward Coke, abolishes a large number. A first bill, passed on May 12, 1621, is rejected by the Lords. It takes until 1624.

## A general ban, and written exceptions

The Statute of Monopolies receives royal assent on May 29, 1624 (legislation.gov.uk files it under the year 1623: the parliamentary session had opened in February 1623, by the old way of dating). Its preamble recalls a royal declaration of 1610 judging such grants unlawful, and notes that they had nonetheless been obtained under false pretenses of public utility, to the harm of the king's subjects. Its first section is radical: monopolies, commissions, licenses, charters and letters patent giving the exclusive right to buy, sell, make, work or use anything in the kingdom are declared contrary to the laws of the realm, and therefore void. Nothing escapes, except what the law itself excepts.

One of these exceptions sits in section VI. It exempts from the general voidness letters patent of fourteen years or less, granted in the future for the exclusive right to make or work any “new Manufacture” within the kingdom, to the “true and first Inventor.” Several conditions frame it: the manufacture must not already be in use by others at the time of the grant; and the privilege must be neither contrary to law nor harmful to the state, whether by raising the price of goods at home, by hurting trade, or by being generally inconvenient.

## An exception that becomes a test

To tell the forbidden privilege from the tolerated one, the text no longer invokes the favor of the prince. It writes conditions: the novelty of the manufacture, the status of first inventor, a limited term, and no harm to trade. A privilege limited in time, reserved for the inventor and refused if it harms trade: the word “patent” does not appear in this section, but the letters patent it preserves already have its outline.

Section VI did not disappear with the era that produced it. According to Wikipedia, it remains the basis of Australian law: the Australian Patents Act of 1990 still refers to a manner of manufacture within the meaning of section 6 of the Statute of Monopolies. In England and Wales, the Patents Act 1977, aligned with the European Patent Convention, implicitly repealed it; yet legislation.gov.uk in 2026 presents sections I, VI, VII and IX as still in force, while sections II to V, VIII and X to XIV are repealed. A text passed to end an abuse thus supplies, through one of its exceptions, the words a modern law still uses to say what an invention is.

repere.texte: Statute of Monopolies: section VI leaves in place letters patent of fourteen years or less granted to the “true and first Inventor” of a new manufacture.
repere.source: Statute of Monopolies, 21 Jac. I, c. 3 (1624), section VI

carte.punch: A law that voids royal monopolies kept a door open for the inventor.
carte.idee: In 1624, the English Parliament voids royal monopolies, but its section VI leaves in place fourteen-year letters patent for the “true and first Inventor” of a new manufacture. Its conditions (novelty, first inventor, limited term) foreshadow the patent.

quiz.question: Why does the Statute of Monopolies of 1624 leave patents for inventions in place while voiding ordinary monopolies?
choix: Because the king kept the power to grant exceptions at will, section VI being only a formality with no real condition
Because the text voided only monopolies already granted, future letters patent remaining free of any condition
Because the text sets precise conditions (a new manufacture, a first inventor, a term of fourteen years at most, no harm to trade) that set this exception apart from an ordinary monopoly
Because only monopolies on goods such as salt or starch were targeted by the ban, industrial processes lying outside the law's scope
quiz.explication: Section VI is not a formality: it limits letters patent to fourteen years or less, reserves them for the true first inventor of a new manufacture that others are not already using, and rules them out if they raise prices, harm trade or are generally inconvenient. It applies to future letters patent, and the ban in section I targets the exclusive right to buy, sell, make, work or use anything, not only salt or starch.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What date does legislation.gov.uk give for the Statute of Monopolies, and why does it differ from the royal assent of May 29, 1624?
choix: 1623, because the parliamentary session had opened in February 1623 by the old way of dating
1625, because the law was applied only after the death of James I
1601, because that is the year of the first showdown between the Crown and Parliament
1621, because that is the date of the first bill rejected by the Lords
quiz_supplementaire.explication: legislation.gov.uk files the law under the year 1623 because the parliamentary session had opened in February 1623, by the old way of dating, whereas the royal assent dates from May 29, 1624.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened to the first bill against monopolies, passed on May 12, 1621?
choix: It received royal assent the same day
It was rejected by the Lords
It was withdrawn by the committee chaired by Edward Coke
It became section VI of the 1624 text without change
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first bill, passed on May 12, 1621, was rejected by the Lords; it took until 1624 for the Statute of Monopolies to receive royal assent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Wikipedia, which country still refers to section VI of the Statute of Monopolies in its patent law today?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, the Australian Patents Act of 1990 still refers to a manufacture within the meaning of section 6 of the Statute of Monopolies.
